newsitem.title: USA: United Kingdom's Blair impresses U.S. bankers.
newsitem.headline: United Kingdom's Blair impresses U.S. bankers.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair told a group of leading U.S. bankers and industrialists on Monday he wanted his ruling Labour Party to be the natural ally of business.
And the movers and shakers present said they liked what they heard.
"They all found him extremely impressive," Callum McCarthy, chief executive officer of the U.S. arm of Britain's Barclay's Bank, told Reuters.

Another participant in the round-table discussion with Blair came away convinced that the man who ended 18 years of Conservative rule when he won power in a landslide on May 1 was a shoo-in for re-election.
"Is he a two-term guy or a three-term guy?" the banker, who declined to be identified, wondered.
Among those invited to the discussion with Blair were the heads of investment banks Morgan Stanley and Salomon Brothers and the vice chairmen of J.P. Morgan, Citibank and Bankers Trust.

Also attending was Stanley Druckenmiller, the managing director of Soros Fund Management, whose founder, George Soros, made a killing at Britain's expense when he correctly speculated that sterling would be forced out of Europe's exchange rate mechanism in September 1992.
Blair did not give away any secrets, but those he met were impressed by his frankness and his readiness to address tricky issues head-on.
"What was refreshing was the clarity and the commitment," said Marshall Millsap, a senior banker who is chairman of the British-American Chamber of Commerce.

Blair explained his plans to improve education and reform Britain's welfare state to ensure everyone is equipped to find work in a rapidly changing economy -- a strategy that steers a course between what he described as outdated state interventionism and unbridled free markets.

"That is a different, a third, way forward from the politics of the past, and I think it gains a lot of support not just in the country but among the business community as well," Blair told reporters before the meeting.

During the meeting, Blair was quizzed about his determination to reshape Britain's welfare system, whose budget of 90 billion pounds ($150 billion) per year is the government's fastest-growing expense.

According to participants, Blair used the comparison of the late U.S. President Richard Nixon's bold stroke in re-stablishing relations with China to illustrate how only a Labour government could drastically reform Britain's welfare state, which it created after the Second World War.
Blair has made a determined effort to woo business both before and since his landslide election victory on May 1.

"I want the Labour party to be the party of business -- the party that says we need a thriving, competitive business sector and that we need to be able to operate effectively in international markets," Blair told reporters before the meeting.
It was his last engagement after a four-day U.S. trip to the annual summit of the Group of Seven industrial nations in Denver and an environmental summit at the the United Nations.

Blair told the executives Labour was now better placed than the Conservatives -- the traditional voice of business in Britain -- to represent British industry and finance because of its more positive stance on Europe.
"Blair's talk went stunningly well -- it was obvious that he was well in command of his facts," John McInestie, a Washington lawyer, said.
One banker at the meeting, asked whether he would still be a buyer of sterling after meeting Blair, even though the pound is now approaching a five-year high, said: "Of course I would. Wouldn't you?"
